chunks: I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: The most beloved of deeds to God, Mighty and Majestic, is salat, and it is the last of the bequests of the Prophets (peace be upon them).
So how excellent is the man who performs ghusl or wudu, and completes the wudu properly, then steps aside to where no one can see him, and God watches over him while he is in ruku' or sajdah!
Indeed when the servant prostrates and prolongs his prostration, Iblees cries out: O woe is me! He obeyed and I disobeyed, and he prostrated and I refused.

key_terms.أَنِيسٌ: A companion/person who might see; the contrast between human observers and divine observation is central to the passage
key_terms.وَصَايَا الْأَنْبِيَاءِ: The bequests/final instructions of the Prophets — emphasizing that salat is a universal prophetic teaching, not merely Muhammadan
key_terms.يُسْبِغُ الْوُضُوءَ: To complete and perfect the wudu — performing all its elements fully and attentively
key_terms.يُشْرِفُ: He oversees/watches from above — used for God's watchful awareness of the worshipper

ai.seo_question: Why is salat the most beloved deed to God according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transmitted a saying he personally heard from an Imam, elevating salat as the most beloved act to God and the final legacy of all the Prophets. The hadith paints a vivid picture of the ideal worshipper — performing full ritual purification privately, away from all observers — watched only by God. It then introduces a striking cosmological scene: Iblees, who once refused to prostrate, laments in anguish every time a servant prolongs his own prostration, making each sajdah a symbolic reversal of the primordial act of disobedience.
